clinicalPearls: IBD is a chronic, idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract; ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) are its two major types (Harrison 22e p.2551).

UC is a mucosal disease that almost always involves the rectum and extends proximally in continuity, without intervening areas of uninvolved (skip) mucosa; ~40-50% have disease limited to rectum/rectosigmoid and ~20% have pancolitis (Harrison 22e p.2555).

CD can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, is segmental with skip areas, and characteristically spares the rectum (unlike UC); the terminal ileum is involved in ~90% of those with small-intestinal disease (Harrison 22e p.2556).

CD is a transmural process producing fistulas, strictures, abscesses and an endoscopic/radiographic 'cobblestone' appearance, whereas UC inflammation is limited to mucosa and superficial submucosa except in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.2555-2556).

Noncaseating granulomas are a characteristic histologic feature of CD but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens; UC shows crypt distortion, basal plasmacytosis, cryptitis and crypt abscesses (Harrison 22e p.2556).

Major UC symptoms are diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, tenesmus, mucus passage and crampy abdominal pain; severe pain is not prominent in UC, whereas CD ileocolitis classically causes right-lower-quadrant pain and diarrhoea, sometimes mimicking acute appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2556-2557).

Perianal disease (perirectal fistulas, fissures, abscesses, anal stenosis, skin tags) occurs in about one-third of CD patients and points away from UC; extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should suggest CD (Harrison 22e p.2556, p.2557).

Faecal calprotectin and faecal lactoferrin are neutrophil-derived markers that correlate with histologic inflammation, help distinguish IBD from irritable bowel syndrome, predict relapse and detect pouchitis; calprotectin is more sensitive for ileocolonic/colonic than isolated ileal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2557, p.2558).
Distinguishing UC from CD is impossible initially in up to 15% of cases (indeterminate colitis); ~5% of resection specimens cannot be classified due to overlapping features (Harrison 22e p.2559).

Up to one-third of IBD patients have at least one extraintestinal manifestation; some parallel bowel activity (erythema nodosum, peripheral arthritis, episcleritis) while others run an independent course (pyoderma gangrenosum, ankylosing spondylitis, sacroiliitis, uveitis, PSC) (Harrison 22e p.2561-2563).

Smoking has opposite associations in the two diseases: it may be protective in UC (OR 0.58) but is a risk factor for CD (OR 1.76); prior appendectomy with confirmed appendicitis is protective against UC but not CD (Harrison 22e p.2551-2552).

Patients with long-standing extensive colitis (UC or Crohn's colitis) have an increased risk of colonic dysplasia and carcinoma; surveillance colonoscopy with multiple biopsies is the standard of care (Harrison 22e p.2612-2613).
harrison.pathophysiology: IBD is regarded as an inappropriate, dysregulated mucosal immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host, shaped by environmental factors. Homeostasis among the commensal microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells and mucosal immune cells is disrupted, producing chronic inflammation. More than ~240 genetic loci (e.g. NOD2, ATG16L1, IL23R, IL12B, IL10, XBP1) contribute incrementally and affect pathways of innate immunity, autophagy/unfolded-protein response, adaptive immunity and inflammation/healing; ~two-thirds are shared between CD and UC. Dysbiosis (e.g. expansion of adherent/invasive E. coli, loss of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) and defective oral (mucosal) tolerance lead to unrestrained CD4+ T-cell (TH1/TH2/TH17) and innate immune activation, with a self-perpetuating cytokine cascade (IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, TNF) driving fibrogenesis, leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage. TH1-driven transmural granulomatous inflammation resembles CD; TH2-type superficial mucosal inflammation resembles UC. Roughly 5-10% of patients have familial disease and only ~20% of disease risk is currently explained by known genetics (Harrison 22e p.2551-2555).
additionalDifferentials: Indeterminate colitis (overlapping UC/CD features in up to 15% of cases)
Ischemic colitis (segmental like CD or diffuse like UC)
Celiac disease (especially in lymphocytic colitis, which should prompt exclusion)
Eosinophilic gastroenteritis, Behcet's syndrome, graft-versus-host disease, neutropenic colitis
infectionMimics: Campylobacter colitis (can mimic severe UC and trigger UC relapse)
Yersinia enterocolitica (terminal ileal ulceration mimicking Crohn's ileitis)
Gonorrhoea, Chlamydia trachomatis and syphilis proctitis
Intestinal tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium (ileocecal involvement)
Cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex colitis/proctitis (may occur even in immunocompetent hosts)
Entamoeba histolytica (amebiasis) - must be excluded before treating presumed IBD
Other parasites: Isospora belli, Trichuris trichiura, hookworm, Strongyloides
Fungal: histoplasmosis, Candida, Aspergillus (mainly in immunocompromised)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug/chemical colitis (phosphosoda, gold, mycophenolate mofetil, cocaine, oral contraceptives)
Neoplasia (lymphoma, carcinoma of colon/ileum, carcinoid, metastatic disease, familial polyposis)
additionalInvestigations: Acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR), platelet count, haemoglobin and serum albumin to gauge activity
Faecal calprotectin and faecal lactoferrin (sensitive markers of intestinal inflammation; distinguish IBD from IBS, predict relapse, detect pouchitis and postoperative recurrence)
Stool studies: bacterial culture, C. difficile toxin, ova and parasites, viral studies to exclude infective colitis
Sigmoidoscopy (to assess activity before treatment) and colonoscopy with multiple biopsies, including terminal ileum
Wireless capsule endoscopy for small-bowel CD (avoid if stricture suspected; consider patency capsule first)
CT enterography or MR enterography (MR preferred in young patients/serial imaging to avoid radiation)
Pelvic MRI for perianal/ischiorectal fistulas and abscesses
Small-bowel ultrasound and intestinal ultrasound for assessing activity and mucosal healing
MRCP (or ERCP) when primary sclerosing cholangitis is suspected
Serologic markers ASCA and pANCA (limited clinical utility; less helpful than clinical factors)
redFlags: Toxic megacolon (transverse or right colon diameter >6 cm with loss of haustration in a severe attack) - may be precipitated by electrolyte abnormalities and narcotics; risk of perforation
Perforation - most dangerous local complication; peritoneal signs may be masked by glucocorticoids; mortality of perforation complicating toxic megacolon is ~15%
Intraabdominal or pelvic abscess and fistula formation (CD); high-spiking fever suggests abscess
Stricture impassable to the colonoscope - presume malignant until proven otherwise
New or worsening dysplasia/carcinoma on surveillance in long-standing colitis
harrison.prognosis: IBD is a lifelong chronic disease with a relapsing-remitting course; only ~15% of UC patients present initially with severe disease. Massive haemorrhage occurs in ~1% of UC patients and toxic megacolon is rare (about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, the remainder requiring urgent colectomy). In CD the inflammatory process tends to evolve toward a fibrostenotic obstructing pattern or a penetrating fistulous pattern; intestinal obstruction occurs in ~40%, intraabdominal/pelvic abscesses in 10-30%, and free perforation in 1-2%. Long-standing extensive colitis carries an increased colorectal cancer risk (UC meta-analysis figures of ~2% at 10 years, 8% at 20 years, 18% at 30 years, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; overall colorectal cancer rates remain ~1.5-2 times the general population). CD and UC cancer risks are probably equivalent for similar extent and duration. Associated PSC carries a 7-10% risk of cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2557-2563, p.2612-2613).
pitfalls: Failing to exclude infective colitis (especially C. difficile, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, CMV) and amebiasis before diagnosing or escalating treatment of IBD - infection can both mimic IBD and trigger relapse (Harrison 22e p.2559-2561).

In UC, biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa are usually abnormal, so multiple biopsies should be taken from apparently uninvolved proximal and distal mucosa; effective medical therapy can also create pseudo-skip areas (Harrison 22e p.2555).
Peritoneal signs of perforation may be absent or subtle in patients on glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.2557).
A colonic stricture impassable with the colonoscope should be presumed malignant until proven otherwise (Harrison 22e p.2557).
Extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's disease (Harrison 22e p.2557).
Wireless capsule endoscopy must be avoided when a small-bowel stricture is suspected because of the risk of capsule retention (Harrison 22e p.2558).
Serologic tests (ASCA, pANCA) have variable predictive value and unclear clinical usefulness for distinguishing or predicting IBD (Harrison 22e p.2559).
Pyoderma gangrenosum and ankylosing spondylitis run a course independent of bowel disease and do not reliably improve with colectomy (Harrison 22e p.2561-2562).
harrison.severityClassification: Ulcerative colitis is graded by the Montreal classification of extent (E1 proctitis; E2 left-sided/distal UC, distal to splenic flexure; E3 extensive/pancolitis, proximal to splenic flexure) and severity (S0 clinical remission; S1 mild: <=4 stools/day with or without blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate: >=4 stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe: >=6 bloody stools/day, pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/100 mL, ESR >=30 mm/h). Crohn's disease is classified by the Vienna and Montreal systems by age at diagnosis (A1/A2/A3), location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper/foregut) and behaviour (B1 nonstricturing-nonpenetrating, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating), with a 'p' modifier for perianal disease (Harrison 22e p.2557-2558).
management: Induce remission with corticosteroids (or aminosalicylates in mild ulcerative colitis) and maintain it with thiopurines, methotrexate or biologics
Escalate to biologic and targeted therapy (anti-TNF agents, anti-integrin vedolizumab, anti-IL-12/23 ustekinumab or JAK inhibitors) for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease
Treat acute severe colitis with intravenous corticosteroids and timely rescue therapy (ciclosporin or infliximab), proceeding to colectomy for toxic megacolon or failure to respond
Offer surgery: colectomy for refractory or dysplastic ulcerative colitis, and resection, stricturoplasty and abscess or fistula management for Crohn's disease
Provide supportive care with nutritional optimisation, correction of iron-deficiency anaemia and smoking cessation in Crohn's disease
Undertake colonoscopic dysplasia surveillance for colorectal cancer and monitor activity with faecal calprotectin and therapeutic drug levels
Manage through a multidisciplinary team of gastroenterology, colorectal surgery and dietetics, with specialist input for extraintestinal manifestations
